content: 1. The roles and responsibilities of all individuals involved in delivering services for people who inject drugs (PWID) must be clearly defined. Additionally, there should be robust systems in place to monitor and evaluate integrated activities at all levels. 2. Education and training programs must focus on building sustainable and effective teams, equipping all personnel who interact with PWID with the necessary skills to manage tuberculosis (TB), HIV, viral hepatitis, drug dependence, and other comorbidities commonly experienced by this population. 3. National programs should develop targeted strategies to enhance the involvement of PWID, non-governmental organizations (NGOs), and civil society organizations in the development and implementation of policies and programs. These strategies should also include advocacy efforts and the monitoring and evaluation of integrated activities at all levels. 4. All stakeholders should actively support operational research to strengthen the evidence base for the efficient, effective, and acceptable delivery of integrated services for PWID. This research should be tailored to the specific context and legal and policy environment. 5. Mediumand long-term joint strategic planning should be developed to systematically scale up integrated services. Joint planning may include the creation of a unified TB, HIV, and viral hepatitis plan for PWID, addressing human rights, legal frameworks, drug and alcohol dependence treatment, needle and syringe programs (NSPs), mental health, and psychosocial needs such as housing. 6. Integrated services should be supported by well-resourced strategies to minimize additional financial input. Streamlined integration can be cost-effective, reduce client time and expenses, and lower excess mortality and morbidity. If programs are underfunded or lack human capacity, additional resources should be mobilized to strengthen them, leveraging funding streams such as the Global Fund or PEPFAR. 7. Adequate staffing and cross-disciplinary training are essential for the provision of integrated services for PWID. Training plans should include pre-service, in-service, and competency-based education for healthcare workers across different programs and sectors, including prisons. Job descriptions should reflect the level of integration required, and specific staff may be appointed to oversee integration efforts. 8. Training for personnel should cover harm reduction principles, patterns of drug use, the relationship between drug use and increased risk of TB, HIV, and viral hepatitis, and non-discriminatory communication with PWID. It should also address drug-drug interactions, side effects of concurrent treatments, and the legal and psychosocial needs of PWID, with appropriate referrals to necessary services. 9. Fear of criminalization and discrimination often prevents PWID from accessing healthcare. NGOs and outreach teams play a critical role in bridging this gap by increasing access to health and social services. 10. Advocacy efforts should focus on influencing policy, sustaining political commitment, and mobilizing resources to accelerate the integrated management of care for PWID. Recognizing and supporting PWID networks is critical for improving service uptake and engagement. 11. Operational research should be encouraged to identify the most effective and context-appropriate models for delivering integrated services. This research should address the burden of disease, optimal service delivery models, and co-management of comorbidities. Researchers must engage meaningfully with PWID and other stakeholders to overcome legal, ethical, and regulatory challenges, ensuring the research is relevant and ethical. 12. Countries should establish specific process and impact targets for scaling up integrated services for PWID to achieve global health goals, such as the Sustainable Development Goals. Monitoring and evaluation systems should be standardized and aligned with global guidance, using harmonized indicators and reporting formats. 13. Integrated service delivery models should be people-centered, addressing the comprehensive needs of PWID, including TB, HIV, viral hepatitis, drug dependence, NSPs, and other services. Stakeholders should collaborate to provide services in a single location whenever possible, ensuring a seamless continuum of care between services, including within prison systems and upon release. 14. Integrated service delivery should address the intertwined nature of conditions such as TB, HIV, and viral hepatitis, as well as their overlapping social and structural determinants. Flexible and coordinated service delivery is essential to reduce barriers to care and improve health outcomes. 15. Facility-based integrated services should involve multidisciplinary teams, including infectious disease specialists, psychiatrists, psychologists, social workers, and nurses, working under combined care protocols. This model enables the provision of comprehensive care, including antiretroviral therapy (ART), opioid substitution therapy (OST), and hepatitis C virus (HCV) services, in one location. 16. Outreach services should integrate drug dependence treatment with TB, HIV, and viral hepatitis services, delivered at a location convenient for the patient. Collaboration between outreach teams, healthcare providers, and housing services allows for tailored treatment in community settings or the patient’s home. 17. Systematic TB screening should be conducted among PWID in settings with high TB prevalence. Adults and adolescents living with HIV should be screened for TB using clinical algorithms, and diagnostic tools such as Xpert MTB/RIF should be used for suspected multidrug-resistant TB or HIV-associated TB. 18. Contact investigation should be conducted for household and close contacts of TB cases, particularly when the index case has smear-positive pulmonary TB, multidrug-resistant TB, or is living with HIV.
